evals.prompt: I'm an Event Manager at Cloudbase, a ~200-person devtools company, and I run our annual user conference. An internal opening just went up on the marketing team titled 'Event Producer' and I can't tell if applying would be a promotion or a step sideways or even down. Can you map out the title ladder in this field for me so I can plan the next five years? I want to end up at director level eventually.
evals.expected_output: A career-path answer that states plainly no universal title ladder exists, lays out the three disagreeing sourced orderings of Producer vs Manager, anchors against the named UK recruiter ladder with its non-tech-native caveat, and advises judging the internal opening by scope rather than title.
expectations: States plainly that no universal title ladder exists across the tech-event-organizing field.
States that three sourced orderings disagree on whether Producer sits above or below Manager.
Presents a data-driven hierarchy that puts Producer below Manager (e.g. Event Specialist -> Event Producer -> Event Manager -> Event Director).
Presents the UK events-recruiter ladder: Junior Producer -> Producer -> Senior Producer -> Conference Manager -> Conference/Divisional Director.
Presents the special-events-industry framing that places Producer at the top as a CEO-equivalent role.
Never declares any single Producer/Manager ordering to be the industry standard.
Labels the UK recruiter ladder as a general B2B conference-industry ladder, not tech-native.
Uses the UK recruiter ladder as an anchor while saying it is not the only correct ordering.

Cites skill-overlap data as the reason titles blur in practice (e.g. Event Manager sharing roughly 79% of core skills with Event Producer, or Director of Event Management sharing roughly 97% with Event Manager).
Advises evaluating the internal Producer opening by its actual scope and day-to-day work rather than by the title.
Notes that in-house tech-company roles often blend producer and manager responsibilities into one hybrid title.
Does not fabricate a tech-conference-specific title ladder.
Mentions heavy cross-functional pull (sales, marketing, product, design) as characteristic of the in-house operating context.

evals.prompt: I'm a project coordinator at a logistics company in Austin and I want to pivot into organizing developer conferences - my dream is working on something like a big cloud vendor's annual dev summit. I have $2,000 of employer L&D budget that expires in December. Everyone on the event-planning subreddits says the move is to get your CMP. Should I spend the budget on CMP prep and the exam?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation that does not default to CMP for a tech-conference target: it explains CMP is real but has no evidenced relevance in tech/developer-conference organizing, that this field is practitioner-credentialed via track record, and redirects the effort toward the volunteer-to-paid path.
expectations: Does not recommend CMP by default for a tech/developer-conference organizing target.
States that no evidence exists that CMP is commonly held, required, or even mentioned by organizers of tech/developer conferences specifically.
States that the sourced examples of CMP's value all come from the corporate-meetings/association/MICE side of the industry.
Acknowledges CMP is a real credential with concrete detail (e.g. 13,000+ holders, an application plus written exam, or 5-year renewal).
States that tech/developer-event organizing skews informal and practitioner-credentialed: a track record of events actually run matters more than a formal certification.
Says CMP may be worth pursuing only for someone targeting the MICE/corporate-meetings side (or a large company's internal MICE-style events org), not as a default step into tech events.
Recommends building a track record of real events (volunteering, self-organized community events) as the higher-leverage use of the effort.
Presents the volunteer-to-paid path as the dominant documented entry path into the field.
Notes that volunteer-to-paid conversion is not automatic and requires actively building a network and asking to meet people in adjacent departments.
Frames volunteer shifts as working interviews (treating every volunteer shift like a job interview).
Does not invent a tech-conference-specific certification as an alternative credential.

evals.prompt: I've been doing DevRel and community work at Ferrostack, a ~400-person dev-tools company, for three years. We run FerroConf, our 1,200-person annual conference, currently owned by a marketing manager who just gave notice. I want to move into owning the conference full-time. Is asking for an internal transfer the standard way people get into event roles, or should I be doing something else?
evals.expected_output: An answer that labels internal transfer as a hypothesis borrowed from the adjacent DevRel field rather than an established route for tech-event roles, names volunteer-to-paid as the documented dominant path, and still endorses attempting the move with a concrete evidence-building plan.
expectations: Labels the internal-transfer route as a hypothesis, not an established or verified entry path for tech-event roles.
States that internal transfer is strongly evidenced as the dominant entry path only in the adjacent DevRel field.
Does not present internal transfer with the same confidence as the volunteer-to-paid path.
Names volunteer-to-paid as the dominant documented entry path in this field.
Still endorses attempting the internal move as worth testing, given the user is already inside a company that runs its own conference.
Notes the volunteer-to-paid evidence comes from general events-industry material, not tech-specific sources.
Recommends assembling a public track record as evidence: named events supported with scale, and metrics such as attendee satisfaction, on-budget delivery, or repeat-attendee rate.
Names the target operating context explicitly as in-house at a tech company.
Notes that in-house roles often blend producer and manager into one hybrid title with cross-functional pull.
Mentions the CMX community-management ladder (or its Developer Relations/Advocacy branch) as a relevant anchor given the user's community-manager-shaped background.
Frames the user's current informal event involvement as evidence to convert deliberately, not as something that converts automatically.
Raises the employer-diligence question of honest scoping: whether one person genuinely owns sponsorship, content, and production for the next edition.

evals.prompt: I have a final-round interview next Thursday at Meshwork, a Series B API platform, for a Developer Community Manager role - I'd own their meetup program across 6 cities plus their annual 500-person developer conference. I already passed two phone screens. Final round is with the VP of Marketing and the recruiter mentioned there will be 'an exercise'. How should I prep?
evals.expected_output: Interview prep built on CMX's five-competency loop with its sample questions, a prediction that the exercise is the paid mini-audit (or sample-thread-response for junior track), a two-length story bank, and employer-diligence questions about the role's real rung.
expectations: Preps the five screened competencies by name: growth mindset, data-driven approach, empathy, leadership, communication.
Includes the pointed conflict question: if the community wants one thing and your boss wants something else, what would you do?
Advises preparing a concrete real example for that conflict question, not a diplomatic non-answer.
States the data-driven competency is assessed by whether the candidate volunteers results and metrics unprompted when describing past projects.
Predicts the exercise is likely a paid mini-audit of the existing community for a senior/final candidate, or names the sample-thread-response exercise as the junior/moderator-track equivalent.
Notes communication is assessed through the depth and quality of follow-up conversation, not a single scripted question.
Recommends banking stories in two lengths: a two-minute version and a thirty-second version.
Story bank includes a live problem troubleshot in real time (a venue change, vendor no-show, or weather contingency).
Story bank includes a real conflict between what a community wanted and what leadership wanted.

Includes at least one more sample competency question, such as 'What are three things you would change about our current community?' or 'How would you respond to a negative comment about the product?'
Recommends employer-diligence questions covering whether a written career matrix exists and which ladder rung this role actually sits at.
States that no single fully-documented tech-conference-specific hiring loop exists published anywhere, so the prep is assembled from general event-industry sources plus a community-management source.

evals.prompt: Torchlane, a cybersecurity vendor in Boston, offered me an Event Marketing Manager role: $112k base plus 10% bonus, running their two-city conference roadshow plus their RSA presence. The recruiter says this is 'above market for event roles.' My friend who works at a nonprofit conference says event people top out around $90k. Who's right, and should I negotiate?
evals.expected_output: An offer evaluation that never blends salary sources into one number: PCMA, BLS, and Glassdoor each cited with their own scope, the IT-industry premium applied to the Event Marketing Manager title specifically, and the friend's figure explained by source scope.
expectations: States that no dev/tech-conference-specific salary survey exists.
Never blends the salary sources into a single market number.
Names the PCMA Convene 2025 Salary Survey with its scope (275 event professionals, primarily North America).
Any PCMA figures used are carried accurately: Coordinator $77,321, Manager $95,077, Director $133,147, Executive/VP $176,217.
Names the US BLS 'Meeting, Convention, and Event Planners' median range of $59,440-$101,310 and flags it as blending every seniority level and industry.
Names Glassdoor's finding that Information Technology is the single highest-paying industry for event titles.
Cites Event Marketing Manager median total pay of $175,690 in IT specifically as the widest tech premium of any title sourced.

Evaluates the recruiter's 'above market' claim against the tech-industry cut, not just the all-industry average (e.g. $112k sits above the ~$100,135 national average for the title but below the IT-specific median).

Explains the friend's ~$90k figure by source scope - a blended all-industry or nonprofit view, with nonprofit/community event pay noted as lower, less standardized, or without sourced bands - rather than dismissing or endorsing it flat.
Attaches a named source (PCMA, BLS, or Glassdoor) to every salary figure quoted.
Recommends negotiating or benchmarking against the IT-industry premium rather than the general average.
Quotes at least one Glassdoor distribution figure for Event Marketing Manager accurately (national average ~$100,135, 75th percentile $127,521, or 90th percentile $157,358).
Does not fabricate a Boston-specific market benchmark; any geographic figures stay within the sourced cuts (San Francisco, New York City) with their caveats.

evals.prompt: I've been a core volunteer organizer of PolyglotDays for four years - it's a community-run nonprofit developer conference that grew from 300 to 2,600 attendees, with a budget around $280k this year. The board is discussing making the organization's first-ever paid hire next year. I run our Discord and all our social channels, so I'm planning to pitch myself as their first paid Community Manager. Good idea? And what should I expect pay-wise?
evals.expected_output: Advice that reshapes the pitch: the first paid hire at community-run events is consistently an event coordinator/manager, never a community manager, so the user should position for that role shape; comp answered honestly as unsourced for this pole rather than extrapolated.
expectations: States that the first paid role at volunteer-community-run events is consistently an event coordinator/manager, never a community-manager role first.
Ties the first-paid-hire threshold to the sourced scale marker - roughly low-thousands of attendees or a six-figure budget - and notes this event has crossed it.
Advises repositioning the pitch toward the coordinator/manager-shaped role rather than a Community Manager title.
Notes that program and community leadership consistently stay volunteer even after the first paid hire.
States that no documented career ladder exists at the non-profit/community pole.
Frames advancement at this pole as succession and bus-factor mechanisms rather than title progression.
States that no sourced salary bands exist specific to non-profit/foundation event-staff pay.
Does not extrapolate a specific salary for this hire from PCMA, BLS, or Glassdoor figures without flagging the scope mismatch; any figure mentioned carries its named source.
Notes compensation at the non-profit/community pole is generally lower and less standardized than the other operating contexts.
Names the operating context explicitly as non-profit/volunteer-community-run.
Answers from the candidate side (how to position for the hire) rather than pivoting into redesigning the organization's governance or team structure.

evals.prompt: I have two offers at roughly the same money. Offer A: Senior Event Producer at Vantage Summit Group - a 30-person company whose entire business is running its own annual fintech conference series. Offer B: Producer at Bright & Klein, an event-production agency with a lot of tech clients. Which is better for a long-term career in tech events? I also toy with the idea of going freelance in a few years.
evals.expected_output: A comparison that names both operating contexts, flags the standing conference business as unsourced (agency-like structure only a hypothesis), gives the agency its documented ladder and freelance-friendly posture, and refuses to assume the contexts transfer.
expectations: States that the standing for-profit conference business context is not sourced - an open question, not something to assume.
If it likens the conference business to an agency (dedicated full-time functions), explicitly flags that as an unverified hypothesis.
States that the event-production agency context has the clearest documented internal ladder of the operating contexts.
Names the agency ladder rungs: Junior Producer -> Producer -> Senior Producer -> Conference Manager -> Director.
Notes agencies specialize roles by function because they serve many clients in parallel.
Connects the user's freelance ambition to the agency path's documented tolerance and reward for a freelance/contractor posture, including the robust freelance market for experienced producers.
Does not assume the day-to-day, ladder, or pay transfers from one operating context to the other.
Names both operating contexts explicitly: a standing for-profit conference business versus an event-production agency.
Recommends employer diligence on the conference-business offer: whether the day-to-day matches the title and whether the role is honestly scoped for a 30-person company.
States that pay data for these contexts is thin: agency bands sourced only as dated UK figures, and no comp data found for a standing for-profit conference business.

evals.prompt: After six years producing internal events at a bank, I'm interviewing for Senior Producer roles at agencies that produce tech conferences. First interview at Kestrel Live in two weeks. My current portfolio is a PDF of event photos plus a list of vendors I've worked with. What should I change about it, and what will the interviews actually look like?
evals.expected_output: A portfolio overhaul and interview forecast built on the general event-planner loop - metrics-backed portfolio review first, scenario questions, budget and stakeholder questions, live reference calls - plus the senior-rung duality differentiator and the cross-sector transferability point.
expectations: States that the consistent first step of the loop is a portfolio and past-events review.
Advises adding concrete metrics to the portfolio: attendee satisfaction scores, percentage of events delivered on-budget, and repeat-client/repeat-attendee rate.
Advises the portfolio show style, scale, and quality level appropriate for the target events, plus client testimonials.
Preps scenario-based questions - a last-minute venue change, a vendor no-show, a weather contingency - framed as testing real-time troubleshooting rather than memorized process.
Preps budget-management questions.
Preps client/vendor-relations questions, including handling a difficult stakeholder.
Warns to expect live reference calls rather than written recommendations.

Presents the senior-rung 'duality' differentiator - research-focused introversion paired with networking extroversion, meticulous detail paired with strategic vision - and warns that presenting only one half reads as under-developed for senior rungs.
Recommends banking interview stories in two lengths (two minutes and thirty seconds).
Notes that recruiters prize transferable production skills across sectors, so the bank background is an asset to present deliberately rather than downplay.
